claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and represents established knowledge about translation.

claims.claim: Changes that disrupt the ability of the mRNA to properly base pair with the cognate tRNA are highly likely to reduce translational speed and fidelity.
claims.source: Changes that disrupt the ability of the mRNA to properly base pair with the cognate tRNA are then highly likely to reduce translational speed and fidelity (Simms et al., 2014; Hudson and Zaher, 2015; Thomas et al., 2019; Hoernes et al., 2018; Hoernes et al., 2016; You et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: O6-methylguanosine (m6G) interferes with the speed and accuracy of decoding when present in mRNA.
claims.source: For example, our group has previously shown that O6-methylguanosine (m6G), which is highly mutagenic during DNA replication, interferes with the speed and accuracy of decoding when present in mRNA.
claims.evidence: This is a reference to previous work by the authors' group.

claims.claim: The effect of m6G on translation depends on its position within the codon.
claims.source: Interestingly, the effect of m6G on translation was found to depend on its position within the codon (Hudson and Zaher, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Given the nature of the decoding process, during which three nucleotides are read simultaneously, modifications to the mRNA can have complex effects on tRNA selection that cannot be solely predicted by their effect on base pairing.
claims.source: These observations suggest that given the nature of the decoding process, during which three nucleotides are read simultaneously, modifications to the mRNA can have complex effects on tRNA selection that cannot be solely predicted by their effect on base pairing.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation about m6G position-dependent effects.

claims.claim: m1A has been found on as much as 20% of the transcriptome depending on the m1A-seq technique used.
claims.source: Depending on the m1A-seq technique used, m1A has been found on as much as 20% of the transcriptome (Dominissini et al., 2016; Li et al., 2016), and as low as nine sites only (Safra et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies using different sequencing methods.

claims.claim: Over half of the identified m1A adducts have been mapped to the coding region of transcripts.
claims.source: Still, regardless of the method used to map the modification, over half of the identified m1A adducts have been mapped to the coding region of transcripts, suggesting that modification is likely to affect ribosome function (Dominissini et al., 2016; Li et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations and includes an inference about ribosome function.

claims.claim: A specific regulatory role of m1A during translation has not been convincingly identified.
claims.source: Notably, a specific regulatory role of this modification during translation has not been convincingly identified.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Studies generally support the hypothesis that m1A exists primarily as a damage adduct that disrupts the decoding process.
claims.source: On the contrary, studies generally support the hypothesis that m1A exists primarily as a damage adduct that disrupts the decoding process (You et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The presence of m1A at any of the three positions within the codon significantly decreased protein-synthesis yield in E. coli translation extracts.
claims.source: This idea is supported by studies conducted using E. coli translation extracts, for which the presence of m1A at any of the three positions within the codon significantly decreased protein-synthesis yield (You et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claims.claim: The addition of the methyl group to the N1 atom of adenosine changes the hydrogen-bond donation and acceptance of the nucleobase.
claims.source: This effect on translation is not unexpected, considering the structure of m1A; the addition of the methyl group to the N1 atom changes the hydrogen-bond donation and acceptance of the nucleobase.
claims.evidence: This is based on established chemical knowledge about the structure of m1A.

claims.claim: The m1A modification introduces a resonance structure with a positive charge to the nucleobase.
claims.source: Furthermore, the modification introduces a resonance structure with a positive charge to the nucleobase.
claims.evidence: This is based on chemical knowledge about the structure of m1A.

claims.claim: The presence of m1A causes local duplex melting in RNA.
claims.source: Consistent with these ideas, the presence of m1A has been shown to cause local duplex melting in RNA (Zhou et al., 2016), and hence would likely occur during codon recognition of tRNA selection.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work, with an inference about codon recognition.

claims.claim: No known methyltransferase that specifically adds m1A to mRNA has been identified.
claims.source: No known methyltransferase that specifically adds m1A to mRNA has been identified.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: m1A and several other adducts are hypothesized to primarily result from reactions between RNA and endogenous and exogenous chemicals.
claims.source: Instead, m1A and several other adducts have been hypothesized to primarily result from reactions between RNA and endogenous and exogenous chemicals (Yan and Zaher, 2019a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: In yeast, the addition of alkylating compounds significantly increases the levels of m1A within mRNA, among several other adducts.
claims.source: In yeast, for example, the addition of alkylating compounds was found to significantly increase the levels of m1A within mRNA, among several other adducts (Yan et al., 2019b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Alkylating compounds activate eukaryotic-quality-control pathways known to be responsible for ribosome rescue in yeast.
claims.source: Interestingly, these compounds were also observed to activate eukaryotic-quality-control pathways known to be responsible for ribosome rescue, suggesting that alkylation stress causes ribosome stalling presumably due to its damaging effect on mRNA.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (implied from context) and includes an inference about the mechanism.

claims.claim: In eukaryotes, ribosome stalling results in ribosome pileup and eventual collisions.
claims.source: Briefly, in eukaryotes, ribosome stalling results in ribosome pileup and eventual collisions.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic quality control pathways.

claims.claim: Collided ribosomes are recognized by an E3 ligase (Hel2 in yeast and ZNF598 in mammals), which adds K63-linked ubiquitin chains to ribosomal proteins.
claims.source: Collided ribosomes are recognized by an E3 ligase (Hel2 in yeast and ZNF598 in mammals), which adds K63-linked ubiquitin chains to ribosomal proteins (Matsuo et al., 2017; Simms et al., 2017b; Saito et al., 2015; Yan and Zaher, 2019c; Ikeuchi et al., 2019; Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2017; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2017; Juszkiewicz et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The ubiquitination is used as a signal to recruit downstream factors involved in mRNA degradation and ribosome splitting.
claims.source: The ubiquitination is used as a signal to recruit downstream factors involved in mRNA degradation and ribosome splitting (Matsuo et al., 2017; Ikeuchi et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The dissociated large-ribosome subunit, still bound to the peptidyl tRNA, is recognized by another E3 ligase (Ltn1 in yeast and listerin in mammals), which adds K48-linked ubiquitin to the nascent peptide.
claims.source: The dissociated large-ribosome subunit, still bound to the peptidyl tRNA, is recognized by another E3 ligase (Ltn1 in yeast and listerin in mammals), which adds K48-linked ubiquitin to the nascent peptide, acting as a signal for its degradation by the proteasome (Bengtson and Joazeiro, 2010; Defenouillère et al., 2013; Brandman et al., 2012; Lyumkis et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Bacteria have evolved entirely distinct mechanisms to deal with stalled ribosomes compared to eukaryotes.
claims.source: Bacteria appear to have evolved entirely distinct mechanisms to deal with stalled ribosomes.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about differences between bacterial and eukaryotic quality control.

claims.claim: The distinction between bacterial and eukaryotic ribosome rescue mechanisms has been hypothesized to be the result of the divergent mechanisms utilized to terminate protein synthesis and recycle the ribosome.
claims.source: This distinction between the two domains of life has been hypothesized to be the result of the divergent mechanisms utilized to terminate protein synthesis and recycle the ribosome (Simms et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: In bacteria, at least four discrete rescue mechanisms have been identified.
claims.source: In bacteria, at least four discrete rescue mechanisms have been identified.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial ribosome rescue pathways.

claims.claim: The tmRNA system appears to be the most widely utilized and conserved rescue pathway in bacteria.
claims.source: Of these, the tmRNA system appears to be the most widely utilized and conserved rescue pathway (Keiler, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: tmRNA contains a transfer RNA segment, which is aminoacylated by Ala-tRNA synthetase.
claims.source: tmRNA or transfer-messenger RNA is a unique molecule in that it contains a transfer RNA segment, which is aminoacylated by Ala-tRNA synthetase; and a messenger mRNA segment, which is used to switch the mRNA template from the defective mRNA to the molecule itself, and hence the name trans translation (Keiler et al., 1996; Moore and Sauer, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Upon ribosome stalling, tmRNA binds the A site of the ribosome in a quaternary complex with elongation factor Tu (EFTu), its partner protein SmpB and GTP.
claims.source: Upon ribosome stalling, tmRNA binds the A site of the ribosome in a quaternary complex with elongation factor Tu (EFTu), its partner protein SmpB and GTP (Valle et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Following peptidyl transfer to tmRNA, the original defective mRNA exits the ribosome, which then begins trans translation whereby the ribosome switches template to the mRNA part of tmRNA.
claims.source: Following peptidyl transfer to tmRNA, the original defective mRNA exits the ribosome, which then begins trans translation whereby the ribosome switches template to the mRNA part of tmRNA (Moore and Sauer, 2007; Gottesman et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The mRNA part of tmRNA encodes a peptide-degradation signal followed by a stop codon, ensuring that the incomplete peptide is degraded by the ClpXP protease system following canonical termination and recycling of the ribosome.
claims.source: This mRNA encodes a peptide-degradation signal followed by a stop codon, ensuring that the incomplete peptide is degraded by the ClpXP protease system following canonical termination and recycling of the ribosome (Keiler and Sauer, 1996).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The tmRNA system has been extensively studied in the context of truncated mRNAs, which result from a myriad of conditions including ribosome stalling.
claims.source: We note that the tmRNA system has been extensively studied in the context of truncated mRNAs, which result from a myriad of conditions including ribosome stalling (Moore and Sauer, 2007), but whether the process is also activated in response to chemical insults that modify RNA is unknown.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and identifies a knowledge gap.

claims.claim: Whether the tmRNA process is activated in response to chemical insults that modify RNA is unknown.
claims.source: We note that the tmRNA system has been extensively studied in the context of truncated mRNAs, which result from a myriad of conditions including ribosome stalling (Moore and Sauer, 2007), but whether the process is also activated in response to chemical insults that modify RNA is unknown.
claims.evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claims.claim: Treating E. coli with common alkylating agents increases the levels of several potentially disruptive alkylative adducts, including m1A.
claims.source: We first demonstrated that treating E. coli with common alkylating agents increases the levels of several potentially disruptive alkylative adducts, including m1A.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: m1A reduces the rate of peptide bond formation by almost three orders of magnitude in a well-defined in vitro translation system.
claims.source: The modification reduced the rate of peptide bond formation by almost three orders of magnitude.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from in vitro translation assays shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The decrease in peptide bond formation caused by m1A is accompanied by a reduction in the endpoint of the peptidyl-transfer reaction, suggesting that the modification affects the proofreading phase of tRNA selection.
claims.source: The decrease in peptide bond formation was also accompanied by a reduction in the endpoint of the peptidyl-transfer reaction, suggesting that the modification affects the proofreading phase of tRNA selection.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data with an inference about the mechanism.

claims.claim: Aminoglycosides, which increase peptide bond formation on mismatched-codon-anticodon interactions, have no effect on reactions with m1A-programmed mRNAs.
claims.source: Highlighting the disruptive effect of m1A on tRNA selection was the observation that aminoglycosides, which increase peptide bond formation on mismatched-codon-anticodon interactions, had no effect on reactions with m1A-programmed mRNAs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Alkylation stress, which increases the levels of disruptive adducts such as m1A, causes widespread stalling in bacterial cells and activates rescue pathways.
claims.source: These findings suggest that alkylation stress, which increases the levels of disruptive adducts such as m1A, causes widespread stalling in bacterial cells and activates rescue pathways.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the in vitro and in vivo data presented.

claims.claim: Robust activation of tmRNA occurs in E. coli cells treated with alkylating agents, even when transcription is inhibited.
claims.source: In complete agreement with these ideas, we documented robust activation of tmRNA in E. coli cells treated with alkylating agents, even when transcription was inhibited.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: DNA damage triggers tmRNA activation, but this activation is significantly suppressed when transcription is inhibited.
claims.source: Interestingly, DNA damage was also found to trigger tmRNA activation, but this activation was significantly suppressed when transcription was inhibited.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Alkylation stress significantly impacts translation through its effect on mRNA and rescue pathways such as trans translation are responsible for dealing with its consequences.
claims.source: Hence, alkylation stress is likely to significantly impact translation through its effect on mRNA and rescue pathways such as trans translation are responsible for dealing with its consequences.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: E. coli strains lacking functional tmRNA are sensitive to alkylating agents and exhibit delayed recovery compared to wild-type cells.
claims.source: Consistent with these proposals, E. coli strains lacking functional tmRNA were found to be sensitive to alkylating agents and exhibited delayed recovery compared to wild-type (WT) cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from growth curve analysis shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Chemical damage to mRNA is highly detrimental to cellular homeostasis, even in organisms where mRNA is highly transient.
claims.source: Collectively our data suggest chemical damage to mRNA is highly detrimental to cellular homeostasis, even in organisms where mRNA is highly transient.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the collective experimental data presented.

claims.claim: The addition of MMS to growing yeast cultures leads to the accumulation of alkylation adducts in RNA.
claims.source: We have recently shown that the addition of methyl methanesulfonate (MMS) to growing yeast cultures leads to the accumulation of alkylation adducts in RNA (Yan et al., 2019b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: MMS alkylates its target through an SN2-type mechanism.
claims.source: MMS alkylates its target through an SN2-type mechanism, while MNNG reacts through an SN1-type one (Wyatt and Pittman, 2006)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work describing the chemical mechanisms.

claims.claim: MNNG reacts through an SN1-type mechanism.
claims.source: MMS alkylates its target through an SN2-type mechanism, while MNNG reacts through an SN1-type one (Wyatt and Pittman, 2006)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work describing the chemical mechanisms.

claims.claim: The ratio of m6A/A levels in untreated E. coli cells has been estimated to be 0.3%.
claims.source: To confirm whether our LC-MS methods are relatively accurate, we measured the ratio of m6A/A levels in untreated cells, which has been estimated to be 0.3% in E. coli (Deng et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The measured ratio of m6A/A in untreated E. coli cells is 0.6%.
claims.source: In agreement with these earlier studies, we measure a ratio of 0.6% (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Treatment with MMS or MNNG does not increase m6A levels in E. coli.
claims.source: Also as expected, we did not detect an increase in m6A levels after treatment with either alkylating agent (Figure 1A), as neither MMS nor MNNG alkylate the N6 position of adenosine (Wyatt and Pittman, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and citation to previous work about the chemical specificity of these agents.

claims.claim: MMS and MNNG react with N1 of G, albeit with reduced efficiency.
claims.source: Additionally, MMS and MNNG have been shown to react with N1 of G, albeit it with reduced efficiency (Wyatt and Pittman, 2006); but we did not observe significant increases in m1G levels (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: m1G is a natural modification of E. coli tRNA and rRNA.
claims.source: These observations can be rationalized by the fact that m1G is a natural modification of E. coli tRNA and rRNA (Machnicka et al., 2013), which significantly increases the background levels of the modification.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The base level of m1G is at least 200-fold higher than that of m1A.
claims.source: Indeed, the base level of m1G is at least 200-fold higher than that of m1A (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: m7G is a natural modification in rRNA and tRNA.
claims.source: Similarly, since m7G is a natural modification in rRNA and tRNA (Machnicka et al., 2013), we observe no significant change to its levels upon MMS and MNNG additions (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Treatment with MMS or MNNG causes 10- to 200-fold increases in m3C and m1A relative levels in E. coli cells.
claims.source: Contrary to m6A and m1G, we measured 10- to 200-fold increases in m3C and m1A relative levels in cells treated with MMS or MNNG (Figure 1D and E)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claims.claim: Treatment with MNNG causes more than tenfold increase in m6G relative levels.
claims.source: and a more than tenfold increase in m6G relative levels but only in those treated with MNNG (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: The O6 position of guanosine is reactive with MNNG but not MMS.
claims.source: These findings are consistent with previous studies showing that the O6 position of guanosine is reactive with MNNG but not MMS and that m3C and m1A are minor alkylative adducts in double-stranded DNA (Beranek, 1990) but are substantially more reactive as nucleophiles in the absence of hydrogen bonding (Bodell and Singer, 1979).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: m3C and m1A are minor alkylative adducts in double-stranded DNA but are substantially more reactive as nucleophiles in the absence of hydrogen bonding.
claims.source: These findings are consistent with previous studies showing that the O6 position of guanosine is reactive with MNNG but not MMS and that m3C and m1A are minor alkylative adducts in double-stranded DNA (Beranek, 1990) but are substantially more reactive as nucleophiles in the absence of hydrogen bonding (Bodell and Singer, 1979).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: N1 of G in single-stranded RNA does not show increased reactivity because it is a secondary amine with an adjacent carbonyl group which is less reactive than N1 of A and N3 of C.
claims.source: This same increase in reactivity for N1 to G in single-stranded RNA is not observed because it is a secondary amine with an adjacent carbonyl group which is less reactive than N1 of A and N3 of C, both of which have the higher reactivity profiles of amidine groups (Wyatt and Pittman, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and chemical knowledge.

claims.claim: The observed rate of peptide bond formation for the Gm1AA complex is 0.15 s−1.
claims.source: The observed rate of 0.15 s−1 for the Gm1AA complex was measured to be more than 250-fold slower relative to the observed rate of 58 s−1 for the unmodified GAA complex.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from in vitro translation assays shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The observed rate of peptide bond formation for the unmodified GAA complex is 58 s−1.
claims.source: The observed rate of 0.15 s−1 for the Gm1AA complex was measured to be more than 250-fold slower relative to the observed rate of 58 s−1 for the unmodified GAA complex.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from in vitro translation assays shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The endpoint of the m1A reaction is approximately tenfold lower relative to the unmodified reaction.
claims.source: Furthermore, the endpoint of the m1A reaction, which reports on the efficiency of proofreading (Pape et al., 1999), was found to be ~tenfold lower relative to the unmodified one (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and citation about what the endpoint represents.

claims.claim: m1A is highly detrimental to the tRNA selection process and is highly likely to stall ribosomes in vivo.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that m1A is highly detrimental to the tRNA selection process and is highly likely to stall ribosomes in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the in vitro experimental data.

claims.claim: During tRNA selection, aa-tRNAs that have only one mismatch between their anticodon and the A-site codon are termed near-cognate.
claims.source: During tRNA selection, aa-tRNAs that have only one mismatch between their anticodon and the A-site codon are termed near-cognate (Gromadski and Rodnina, 2004a).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: The addition of certain aminoglycosides alters the selection process and allows for the misincorporation of near-cognate aa-tRNAs.
claims.source: Although the ribosome efficiently discriminates against the incorporation of near-cognate aa-tRNAs, the addition of certain aminoglycosides alters the selection process and allows for their misincorporation (Pape et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Paromomycin binds the decoding center of the ribosome, which leads to local conformational changes that lower the energy barrier required to shift the ribosome into a 'closed' conformation.
claims.source: For instance, paromomycin binds the decoding center of the ribosome, which leads to local conformational changes that lower the energy barrier required to shift the ribosome into a 'closed' conformation (Fourmy et al., 1996; Ogle et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The closed conformation typically occurs in the presence of cognate aa-tRNAs and is a prerequisite for their accommodation into the active site of the ribosome for peptidyl transfer to take place.
claims.source: This conformation typically occurs in the presence of cognate aa-tRNAs and is a prerequisite for their accommodation into the active site of the ribosome for peptidyl transfer to take place (Ogle et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The addition of aminoglycosides to reactions containing non-cognate aa-tRNAs has little to no effect on peptide bond formation.
claims.source: By contrast, the addition of aminoglycosides to reactions containing non-cognate aa-tRNAs, which harbor more than one mismatch between their anticodon and the A-site codon, has little to no effect on peptide bond formation (Pape et al., 2000; Gromadski and Rodnina, 2004b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The addition of paromomycin and streptomycin de-represses the effects of the oxidative adduct 8-oxoguanosine (8-oxoG) on peptide bond formation.
claims.source: For instance, we recently showed that the addition of paromomycin and streptomycin de-represses the effects of the oxidative adduct 8-oxoguanosine (8-oxoG) on peptide bond formation (Thomas et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: The ribosome recognizes 8-oxoG as a simple mismatch when paired with its partner nucleotide.
claims.source: These findings suggest that the ribosome recognizes this modification as a simple mismatch when paired with its partner nucleotide.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the effect of aminoglycosides on 8-oxoG.

claims.claim: In the presence of m1A, the addition of paromomycin has little to no effect on the observed rate of peptide bond formation.
claims.source: Interestingly and in contrast to 8-oxoG, in the presence of m1A, we found the addition of paromomycin to have little to no effect on the observed rate of peptide bond formation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The observed rate of peptide bond formation in the presence of m1A is 0.15 s−1 without paromomycin and 0.2 s−1 with paromomycin.
claims.source: In particular, we measured observed rates of 0.15 s−1 and 0.2 s−1 in the absence and presence of an antibiotic, respectively (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The endpoints of reactions with m1A are 0.10 without paromomycin and 0.11 with paromomycin.
claims.source: Additionally, the endpoints of the very same reactions were 0.10 and 0.11, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the same experiments shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: m1A is unable to base pair with U in the decoding center and significantly distorts the codon-anticodon helix.
claims.source: These findings suggest that not only is m1A unable to base pair with U in the decoding center but that the modification significantly distorts the codon-anticodon helix.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect of paromomycin on m1A-containing reactions.

claims.claim: The distortion caused by m1A results in the aa-tRNA, that is otherwise cognate, to be recognized as a non-cognate one by the ribosome.
claims.source: This distortion results in the aa-tRNA, that is otherwise cognate, to be recognized as a non-cognate one by the ribosome.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect of paromomycin on m1A-containing reactions.

claims.claim: For the codon containing unmodified adenosine, no significant dipeptide accumulation occurs except in the presence of the cognate Glu-tRNAGlu ternary complex.
claims.source: As anticipated, for the codon containing the unmodified adenosine, we observed no significant dipeptide accumulation except in the presence of the cognate Glu-tRNAGlu ternary complex (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: For the codon containing m1A, no significant dipeptide accumulation occurs in the presence of any aa-tRNA.
claims.source: For the codon containing m1A, no significant dipeptide accumulation occurred in the presence of any aa-tRNA.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The m1A modification inhibits base pairing altogether and does not alter the base-pairing preference of the nucleotide.
claims.source: These findings strongly suggest that the modification inhibits base pairing altogether and does not alter the base-pairing preference of the nucleotide.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the aa-tRNA reactivity survey data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Two- to threefold increases in His6-tagging levels occur upon the addition of MMS and MNNG to E. coli expressing tmRNA-His6.
claims.source: Consistent with our proposal that alkylation stress activates the tmRNA system, we observed two- to threefold increases in His6-tagging levels upon the addition of MMS and MNNG to E. coli expressing tmRNA-His6 (Figure 5A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claims.claim: The increase in tmRNA activity upon alkylation stress is accompanied by activation of the adaptive response as judged by the accumulation of Ada protein.
claims.source: As expected, this increase in tmRNA activity was accompanied by activation of the adaptive response as judged by the accumulation of Ada protein, the principal mediator of the process in response to alkylation damage (Jeggo, 1979; Sakumi and Sekiguchi, 1989; Uphoff et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Activation of the SOS response occurs upon alkylation stress as evaluated by the accumulation of RecA.
claims.source: We also observe activation of the SOS response as evaluated by the accumulation of its principal mediator RecA (Cox, 2007)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: At 0.1% MMS concentration and 20 min treatment duration, there is little to no effect on cellular viability.
claims.source: It is worth noting that at this concentration of MMS and duration of treatment, we observe little to no effect on cellular viability as assessed by spot assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Under normal conditions, His-tagged products resulting from tmRNA activation are targeted for degradation by the ClpAP, ClpXP, and Lon proteases.
claims.source: Under normal conditions, His-tagged products resulting from tmRNA activation are targeted for degradation by the ClpAP, ClpXP, and Lon proteases, presumably because they are incomplete peptides that are likely to misfold.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the fate of tmRNA-tagged proteins.

claims.claim: Previous reports have shown the deletion of ΔclpP, clpX, and lon genes to result in increased accumulation of His-tagged products.
claims.source: Indeed, previous reports have shown the deletion of ΔclpP, clpX, and lon genes to result in increased accumulation of His-tagged products (Moore and Sauer, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The levels of His-tagging triggered by the addition of alkylation compounds increased by more than twofold in the absence of ClpP, ClpX, and Lon proteases.
claims.source: As expected, the levels of His-tagging triggered by the addition of alkylation compounds increased by more than twofold in the absence of these proteases (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

results.result: Treatment of E. coli with alkylating agents MMS and MNNG leads to significant increases in specific RNA modifications, particularly m1A and m3C, while other modifications like m6A and m1G remain unchanged or show minimal increases. LC-MS analysis demonstrates 10- to 200-fold increases in m1A and m3C levels, and MNNG specifically causes >10-fold increase in m6G levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C39, C59, C60 are directly supported by LC-MS data in Figure 1 showing quantitative increases in specific modifications. The chemical specificity (C50, C51, C61, C62, C63) is supported by citations to established chemistry literature. The measured m6A/A ratio of 0.6% (C53) validates the LC-MS methodology against the expected 0.3% (C52). The differential reactivity patterns between MMS and MNNG (C118, C119) are consistent with their known SN2 vs SN1 mechanisms.

results.result: m1A modification in mRNA reduces the rate of peptide bond formation by approximately 250-fold (from 58 s⁻¹ to 0.15 s⁻¹) and decreases the reaction endpoint by ~10-fold in a reconstituted in vitro translation system, demonstrating that m1A is highly detrimental to tRNA selection.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C40, C64, C65, C66, C120 are directly supported by quantitative kinetic data shown in Figure 2C from well-controlled in vitro peptidyl transfer assays. The experimental design appropriately compares modified and unmodified mRNA under identical conditions. The magnitude of the effect (three orders of magnitude) and the reduction in endpoint are clearly documented with replicate measurements.

results.result: m1A modification causes such severe distortion of the codon-anticodon helix that paromomycin, which normally rescues near-cognate tRNA incorporation, has no effect on peptide bond formation rates or endpoints. This indicates m1A prevents base pairing altogether and causes all aa-tRNAs to be recognized as non-cognate.
results.evaluation: Claims C42, C75, C76, C77, C122 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing no paromomycin effect on m1A-containing reactions. The inference that m1A causes severe distortion (C78, C79, C123) is well-justified by comparison to the known mechanism of paromomycin action (C69-C72) and the aa-tRNA reactivity survey data in Figure 4 (C80, C81, C82, C124). The logic connecting lack of paromomycin rescue to non-cognate recognition is sound.

results.result: Alkylating agents robustly activate the tmRNA system in E. coli, as evidenced by 2- to 3-fold increases in His6-tagging levels, accompanied by activation of adaptive (Ada) and SOS (RecA) responses. This activation occurs at concentrations that do not significantly affect cellular viability and is enhanced in protease-deficient strains.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C44, C83, C125 are directly supported by Western blot data in Figure 5A-B showing increased His-tagging. The accompanying stress responses (C84, C85) are documented in the same figure. The viability data (C86) from Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B validates that the observed effects are not due to cell death. The protease-deficient strain data (C89, C90) from Figure 5—figure supplement 2 confirms that observed His-tagging underestimates true tmRNA activity.

results.result: tmRNA activation by alkylating agents is predominantly due to direct RNA damage rather than truncated transcripts from DNA damage, as demonstrated by rifampicin pretreatment experiments showing only 10-20% reduction in His-tagging for MMS/MNNG but ~2-fold reduction for ciprofloxacin.
results.evaluation: Claims C92, C94 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5C showing differential effects of rifampicin pretreatment on different damaging agents. The inference that tmRNA activation is primarily due to RNA damage (C93, C96, C127) is well-justified by the experimental design: rifampicin blocks new transcription, so persistent tmRNA activation must result from damage to existing mRNA. The ciprofloxacin control (C94) appropriately demonstrates that DNA damage-induced truncated transcripts do activate tmRNA but are blocked by rifampicin.

results.result: In cell-free translation systems, MMS-treated mRNA shows reduced full-length product and significantly activates tmRNA tagging, demonstrating that damaged mRNA directly causes ribosome stalling and tmRNA recruitment in the absence of transcription.
results.evaluation: Claims C97, C99, C100 are directly supported by experimental data in Figure 6C showing both reduced full-length product (35S-labeling and FLAG Western blot) and increased His-tagging (His Western blot) with MMS-treated mRNA. The inference about stalling (C98) is reasonable given the reduced full-length product. This experiment provides strong support for the model by eliminating transcription-related confounders.

results.result: m1A-modified mRNA accumulates to higher levels in ΔssrA cells compared to wild-type cells following MMS treatment, as detected by m6A immunoblotting after base treatment to convert m1A to m6A, suggesting tmRNA facilitates degradation of damaged mRNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C104, C105 are supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B showing increased signal in the mRNA size range after base treatment in ΔssrA cells. The inference that tmRNA facilitates mRNA degradation (C106) is reasonable given the established role of tmRNA in recruiting RNase R (C102). However, the indirect detection method (m1A→m6A conversion) and inability to purify bacterial mRNA introduce some uncertainty about the specificity of the signal.

results.result: E. coli strains lacking functional tmRNA (ΔssrA) exhibit delayed recovery (~1.5 hr lag) after treatment with alkylating agents compared to wild-type cells, without differences in cell death, indicating that trans-translation is important for rapid recovery from alkylation stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C47, C108, C135 are directly supported by growth curve data in Figure 7 showing delayed recovery in ΔssrA strains. The viability data (C109) from Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-D appropriately controls for differential cell death. The inference that the lag reflects inability to rescue stalled ribosomes (C110, C111) is well-justified by the totality of evidence showing tmRNA activation and ribosome stalling on damaged mRNA.

results.result: The authors propose that translation is exceptionally sensitive to chemical changes in mRNA, that alkylation stress causes widespread ribosome stalling necessitating rescue pathways, and that bacteria have evolved to monitor mRNA chemical integrity through trans-translation.
results.evaluation: While C1 is stated as a hypothesis, the collective experimental evidence from in vitro translation (showing 250-fold reduction in peptide bond formation), in vivo tmRNA activation, and delayed recovery in ΔssrA strains provides strong support for the overall model (C4, C43, C46). The broader conclusions about bacterial monitoring of mRNA integrity (C6, C48) are well-justified inferences from the data, though they represent interpretive claims rather than direct observations.

results.result: The manuscript establishes background knowledge about aminoglycoside effects on tRNA selection, including that paromomycin allows near-cognate but not non-cognate tRNA incorporation, and that 8-oxoG is recognized as a simple mismatch based on paromomycin rescue.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C72 are well-established facts about ribosome decoding and aminoglycoside mechanisms, supported by appropriate citations to the literature. Claims C73-C74 reference the authors' previous work on 8-oxoG, which provides important context for interpreting the m1A results. This background is accurately presented and appropriately cited.

results.result: The introduction establishes relevant background about RNA susceptibility to damage, the importance of Watson-Crick base pairing in translation, previous work on m1A and m6G modifications, and the hypothesis that m1A exists primarily as a damage adduct rather than a regulatory modification.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C24 represent background knowledge and literature review appropriately supported by citations. The characterization of m1A as primarily a damage adduct (C15, C16, C21, C22) is well-supported by cited literature and the lack of identified methyltransferases. The chemical properties of m1A (C18, C19, C20) are established facts. This background appropriately frames the current study.

results.result: The manuscript provides comprehensive background on eukaryotic and bacterial ribosome rescue mechanisms, including the eukaryotic RQC pathway and the bacterial tmRNA system, noting that whether tmRNA responds to chemical RNA damage was previously unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C36 accurately describe established mechanisms of ribosome rescue in eukaryotes and bacteria, appropriately supported by citations. The identification of the knowledge gap (C37, C38) appropriately motivates the current study. This background is accurately presented and provides essential context for understanding the significance of the findings.

results.result: The discussion contextualizes findings within existing knowledge about mRNA modifications, tmRNA function, protease degradation of tagged proteins, alternative rescue factors, and technical limitations of studying bacterial mRNA, while noting that the response to alkylation is likely general and that alternative rescue factors probably enable eventual recovery in ΔssrA cells.
results.evaluation: These claims represent appropriate contextualization of the findings (C112-C117), discussion of technical considerations (C128-C133), and reasonable inferences about mechanisms (C87, C88, C91, C101-C103, C107, C134, C136-C139). The discussion appropriately addresses limitations (inability to definitively prove mRNA vs rRNA/tRNA damage) while providing logical arguments for why mRNA is the primary target. The inference about alternative rescue factors (C139) is well-justified by cited literature.

results.result: An aa-tRNA reactivity survey demonstrates that unmodified GAA codon shows dipeptide formation only with cognate Glu-tRNAGlu, while m1A-containing codon shows no significant dipeptide formation with any aa-tRNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C80 and C81 are directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4. The survey appropriately tests all 20 aa-tRNAs and provides clear evidence that m1A prevents productive interactions with any tRNA. This result strongly supports the conclusion that m1A completely disrupts base pairing.
